I am 68 years old, and my bones ache when the weather turns, but I know every corner of these 4.5 mu like the back of my hand. My wife and I tend the farm alone now—our children work in the city and send money home, but the land is still our responsibility. With only two of us and my strength not what it used to be, I cannot afford to waste labor or money on fancy methods. I stick to what 25 years of planting wheat and maize in Quzhou has taught me.

My wheat went into the ground last autumn, as it always does. I buy improved wheat seed from the county supply store—reliable, not too expensive, and I have saved some of my own seed before, but the improved varieties resist disease better. Before planting, I rotary till the soil to break up the corn stubble and level the field. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer as a base before sowing, then topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. I do not overdo it—fertilizer prices have risen, and too much makes the wheat lodge. My well pump gives me water when the rains fail, which they often do. I will irrigate three times for the wheat: once when it greens up in spring, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. That is enough. I spray herbicide once in early spring for the weeds, and if I see aphids or rust, I spray once more. I expect about 420 kg per mu from the wheat if the weather holds.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I plant maize. There is no time to plough—the summer season is short, and the soil is still moist from the wheat harvest. I plant hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble with minimal tillage. Hybrid seed costs more, but the yield difference pays for itself. I give the maize a base dressing of compound fertilizer and topdress with urea when the plants are knee-high. I irrigate twice: once when it is jointing, and once at filling. The summer rains usually help, so two times from the well is sufficient. I spray herbicide after emergence, and if the corn borers appear, I spray insecticide once. I expect around 520 kg per mu for the maize.

I keep things simple because at my age, complicated plans lead to mistakes. I watch the sky, I walk the fields every morning, and I adjust if the season is dry or wet. But this is my plan.
